questions.question:
**In the sentence identify the segment which contains the grammatical error.**

Are you having your own transport to go home from work?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 3 i.e. Are you having.

The error is in the first part of the sentence and it has to be modified.

‘Have’ should always be in the simple present tense for the meaning “to own”, or to describe medical problems. For example: *They have a new car. I have a bad cold. *It is incorrect to say “I am having a cold” or “I am having a new car.”

We use do/does or is/are as question words when we want to ask yes/no questions.

Hence the phrase “Are you having” should be replaced with “Do you have”.

__Correct sentence__: *Do you have your own transport to go home from work?*

Highways are a catalyst for economic growth but private ______ in this sector has been termed 'tardy' as investors do not appear to be interested in putting their money in long-term projects.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 4 i.e. investment.

Let us look at the meanings first:

__

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.**

This college is not only equipped with the best laboratories __but also has the most__ competent staff.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 3 i.e. No improvement.

‘Not only...but also’ are a pair of correlative conjunctions. It is used to present two related pieces of information. Both pieces of information are being presented by the writer as surprising or unexpected, with the second one being even more surprising than the first. The first piece of information, which we’ll call [A], comes after *not only*, and the second piece of information, [B], comes after *but* also.

Correlative conjunctions come in pairs, and you have to use both of them in different places in a sentence to make them work. They get their name from the fact that they work together (co-) and relate one sentence element to another. Correlative conjunctions include pairs such as "both/and", "either/or", "neither/nor" and "not/but".

The rest of the sentence is also grammatically correct and does not have to be improved.

questions.question:
**In the sentence identify the segment which contains the grammatical error.**

If the growth of population had been controlled earlier, mankind wouldn't lived in a polluted world now.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2 i.e. mankind wouldn't lived.

The error is in the third part of the sentence and it has to be modified.

The first half of the sentence is correct. The past perfect passive tense has been used- *had been controlled*. The Past Perfect Passive has the exact same meaning as the Past Perfect Tense. The past perfect tense form is made by putting had before the past participle form of the verb. The past perfect tense in the passive voice is made by putting* had been* before the past participle form of the verb.

Active form: had + past participle form of the verb

Passive form: had been + past participle form of the verb

**In the second half of the sentence, ‘mankind wouldn’t lived’ has to be replaced. We have to use the Present Continuous Conditional tense here. This form is common in Type 2 conditional sentences.** It expresses an unfinished or continuing action or situation, which is the probable result of an unreal condition. Eg: I would be working in Italy if I spoke Italian (but I don’t speak Italian, so I am not working in Italy).

 
 

 **Subject**
 **would be**
 **base + -ing**
 
 

 he
 would be
 going
 
 

 we
 would be (affirmative)
 working
 
 

 we
 wouldn't be (negative)
 working
 
 

 

Hence the phrase “mankind wouldn’t lived” should be replaced with “mankind wouldn’t be living”.

__Correct sentence____:__ *If the growth of population had been controlled earlier, mankind wouldn't be living in a polluted world now.*

questions.question: What probably caused the greatest excitement among the children?

options.text: Learning that the school would be closed
Seeing a tiger getting into the school
Watching the tiger run after them
Knowing the tiger was coming to eat them

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1. 

In the 1st paragraph of the passage, it is said that schools being closed hurriedly delighted the children. They were also shouting joyously “No school, no school. Tiger, tiger!" 

This indicates that learning that the school would be closed was more exciting to them than seeing a tiger wandering around.

questions.question: What was the tiger’s reaction to the frenzy around him?

options.text: He wanted to go back to his cave.
He looked for someone to attack.
He was afraid of being caught.

questions.solution: The correct answer is option 1.

questions.question: Where was the tiger just before he ran towards the school?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 3. 

In the 1st paragraph of the passage, notice the line “I felt like joining them, and bounded away from the restaurant door.” This is the tiger’s first reaction when he sees everyone running helter-skelter. So, he was first near a restaurant’s door and then he followed the children into the school.

questions.question: Which word describes the tone of the narrative when the headmaster’s reaction to the tiger’s arrival is mentioned?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1. 

In the 2nd paragraph of the passage, notice the line “a very dignified man jumping on his table and heaving himself up into an attic.” When we imagine a headmaster, we picture a very serious and respectable man in formal clothing. The portrayal of someone in this manner trying to hoist himself up into an attic is amusing. 

Hence, the tone of the narrative is Humorous.

questions.question: What did a mischievous person say about the headmaster?

options.text: He should keep the school closed for some time
He should allow the tiger to sleep peacefully.
The school would be better managed by the tiger than by him.
He should leave the place and go because of his fear of the tiger.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 3. 

In the 2nd paragraph of the passage, we find that the tiger got into the headmaster’s office and just lay there while the headmaster upon seeing him tried to escape into the attic. Soon the tiger was alone in the room and its doors were locked. The tiger had effectively taken the room from the headmaster and he later remarks "Never dreamt in my wildest mood that I'd have to yield my place to a tiger." Then someone retorts that a tiger taking his place might be the only way of maintaining better discipline among the boys. This suggests that the headmaster is not strict with his students and they are not that scared of him.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1 i.e. Very.

The meanings of the given options are:

 
• Very: in a high degree
 
• So: to such a great extent
 
• Too: to a higher degree than is desirable, permissible, or possible; excessively
 
• Much: a large amount

‘Too’, ‘so’, and ‘very’ are similar words but we use them differently. 

Too + adjective is used to show something is excessive or problematic. Too is used with negative adjectives like expensive, tired, difficult, etc. Too implies a negative feeling and perhaps an unstated negative consequence: It’s too hot today(This implies that it is hot and there is some negative feeling or problem)

So + adjective is similar to too, but it can be used with positive or negative adjectives. So is used to show a cause and effect relationship. So is often used with that: I’m so excited about my vacation that I can’t sleep.

When we simply want to emphasize an adjective, we use very. Very + adjective makes that adjective stronger: Angelina is very beautiful.

In the above paragraph, to emphasise that polar bears are really strong swimmers, we use ‘very’ as the adverb.

• Them: used as the object of a verb or preposition to refer to two or more people or things previously mentioned or easily identified. “she was expecting them in the evening”
 
• Whom: used instead of ‘who’ as the object of a verb or preposition."whom did he marry?"

In the above passage, ‘which’ in the 2nd blank refers to the large paws of the polar bears.

questions.question:
In the sentence identify the segment which contains the grammatical error.

Only one copy of the book, running into 1200 pages, on Gandhiji's visit to the State of Andhra Pradesh, remain now.

options.text: on Gandhiji's visit to the State
Only one copy of the book

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1 i.e. remain now.

‘Remain now’ is incorrect as ‘remain’ is plural. It has to be replaced with ‘remains’ which is a singular form of the verb. The subject of the sentence is singular- one copy of the book. Since the subject is singular, the verb has to be singular too, according to the Subject-Verb Agreement rule. If the subject is plural, then the verb should also be plural.

__Correct sentence__: Only one copy of the book, running into 1200 pages, on Gandhiji's visit to the State of Andhra Pradesh, *remains *now.
